extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, experimentalists, philosophers of science
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the core methods for discovering causal laws by varying circumstances: the practical distinction between observation and experiment, and the Method of Agreement and Method of Difference for isolating causes and effects. Intended as guidance for designing, interpreting, and assessing inductive/experimental investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baconian rule of varying the circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: We are to inquire which antecedent is connected with which consequent by meeting with some antecedents apart from the rest, or some consequents apart from the rest; in short, follow the Baconian rule of varying the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as 'the foundation of all the rest' of physical inquiry: to distinguish real laws and assign causes to effects we must be able to observe antecedents or consequents separately. Practical implementation requires seeking instances where particular antecedents or consequents occur apart from other confounding circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between observation and experiment based on feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: For varying the circumstances we may have recourse either to observation (finding an instance in nature) or to experiment (artificially arranging circumstances); there is no difference in kind but practical distinctions matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When phenomena can be produced artificially, experiment is preferred because it enables controlled variation; when they cannot (e.g., human mind, society, astronomy) one must rely on observation and possibly deduction. The page emphasizes assessing whether artificial production of the antecedent is possible before deciding methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation as an extension of observation (control and precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimentation is an immense extension of observation: it enables production of far more and more precise varieties of circumstances than nature provides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments can produce the precise variation needed to discover laws (example: isolating atmospheric gases to discover oxygen supports respiration). When a phenomenon can be produced artificially, the experimenter can 'take it home' and observe it amid known circumstances, controlling concomitant factors and introducing well-defined changes one by one (examples: electrical machine, galvanic battery, chemical manipulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation of concomitant circumstances for causal inference
rubrics_metrics.description: When we can produce a phenomenon artificially we can determine, so far as compatible with its nature, the whole of the circumstances present along with it, and observe what alteration is made by the presence of the antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits introducing one well-defined circumstance after another and obtaining assurance how the phenomenon behaves under varied conditions (chemists introducing reagents, applying heat/electricity/pressure). The ability to know the simultaneous state of everything else is crucial for attributing effects to causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation without experiment cannot by itself prove causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation, without experiment (and without aid from deduction), can ascertain uniformities but cannot prove causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An observed invariable antecedence (A always preceding a) might be only an invariable sequence (like day and night) rather than causation; to establish causation one must reverse the process and produce the effect by means of the antecedent (add experimental evidence). The text warns that observation alone may establish uniformities but leaves the question of causation undecided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement (FIRST CANON)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more instances of the phenomenon under investigation have only one circumstance in common, the circumstance in which alone all the instances agree, is the cause (or effect) of the given phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this by comparing different instances where the phenomenon occurs; the common circumstance is an invariable antecedent or consequent. Example: comparing instances that all share deposition from a liquid to infer crystallization's invariable antecedent. Caveat: Method of Agreement yields uniformities but not necessarily causes unless the antecedent can be produced and the effect observed (i.e., combined with Method of Difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference (SECOND CANON)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an instance in which the phenomenon occurs, and an instance in which it does not occur, have every circumstance save one in common, that one occurring only in the former, the circumstance in which alone the two instances differ, is the effect, or cause, or a necessary part of the cause, of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method compares an occurrence with a non-occurrence differing only by one factor (relation AB C vs B C). It is particularly powerful for experimental situations where the experimenter can ensure the two instances are identical except for the candidate antecedent. Example: establishing that a gunshot (difference) killed a man. Requires careful control to ensure no other unobserved change occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods as procedures of elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Both Method of Agreement and Method of Difference operate by elimination: successively exclude circumstances found to be compatible with the phenomenon; what remains is implicated by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method of Agreement uses elimination by showing what can be absent without prejudice to the phenomenon; Method of Difference uses elimination by showing what cannot be excluded without preventing the phenomenon. Framing experiments to eliminate non-causal factors is central to both methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference requires stricter identity of comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The two instances compared must be exactly similar in every other respect except the one circumstance being tested (they must be in the relation ABC and BC, or abc and bc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strict similarity is seldom available in spontaneous natural instances due to complexity and multiplicity of factors; it is much easier to achieve in artificial experiments where a previous state BC is known and A is introduced rapidly. The text notes that known-immaterial circumstances may be ignored, but generally careful matching is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement is chiefly for situations where experiment is impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of Agreement does not require special pairings of instances and can be used on any instances in which nature presents the phenomenon; hence it is the resource where experimentation is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It can identify invariable antecedents or consequents across many diverse cases (ABC, ADE, AFG → A is associated) but cannot by itself determine causation; best used to suggest hypotheses for subsequent experimental testing by Method of Difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty about causes requires producing antecedent and observing consequent
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that an antecedent is the cause of a consequent, we must reverse the process and produce the effect by means of that antecedent (i.e., add experimental evidence to observation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: producing crystals by keeping a charged solution undisturbed; Sir James Hall producing artificial marble. Only when an antecedent is produced under known circumstances and the consequent follows can causation be asserted with confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations when phenomena cannot be artificially produced
rubrics_metrics.description: In sciences dealing with phenomena that cannot be produced artificially (astronomy) or only in limited ways (physiology, mental philosophy, social science), induction from direct experience is often at a disadvantage equivalent to impracticability, so methods must be largely deductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises recognizing where observation is inherently limited (e.g., human mind, societies) and adjusting expectations about what direct induction can achieve; reliance on deduction or other methods may be necessary for progress in such fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of attributing effects to means of production
rubrics_metrics.description: When producing an antecedent artificially one must consider that the observed effect might have been generated not by the antecedent itself but by the means employed to produce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This possibility can often be tested by varying the means and seeing whether the same effect occurs; the experimenter must ensure that causal attribution is not confounded by the method of manipulation (example caveat given in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method selection: Agreement suggests hypotheses, Difference verifies causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Agreement is chiefly to be resorted to as a means of suggesting applications of the Method of Difference; the latter is the instrument by which we can arrive with certainty at causes in direct experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Agreement to detect candidate antecedents/common features across diverse cases, then design Difference-style experiments (or observations where possible) to test whether the candidate antecedent, when isolated, produces the effect. The two methods are complementary parts of experimental inquiry.
